metadata.title: Civic Education Outcomes After Emergency Lockdowns: International Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 and ICCS 2022 Grade 8 data, which come from a stratified two-stage cluster design (schools selected with probability proportional to size, then classrooms sampled). The authors state that all analyses apply sampling weights and that, in pooled analyses across countries, senate weights are used so each country contributes equally regardless of sample size. Standard errors are computed using jackknife repeated replication to account for sampling variance under the complex design. Because the models are regression-based (not ML algorithms), the paper explicitly incorporates the survey design via these weights and replicate variance estimation rather than omitting weights.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample is restricted to countries (and one benchmarking subnational entity, Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia) that participated in both ICCS 2016 and ICCS 2022. The outcomes are ICCS Grade 8 civic scales (civic knowledge via rotated booklet PVs; trust and expected participation scales via IRT-based scales) linked across cycles. The study uses country-level COVID-19 containment measures from OxCGRT aggregated from the start of 2020 to February 2022 (with weekends and academic holidays removed for the school-closure duration measure). For missing data, the paper reports that missing values for independent variables were handled via a separate missing category/code (and an indicator for continuous variables), while missingness on the dependent variable led to casewise deletion.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Separate regressions (standardized coefficients, jackknife SEs). Avg. Stringency: −0.035*** (SE 0.010); Days Closed: −0.041*** (SE 0.011). # Students: 107,995 (CIVKNO).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Civic Knowledge the study leveraged student demographics and country-level pandemic severity controls to estimate how COVID-19 lockdown stringency and school-closure duration relate to changes in civic knowledge, finding that greater lockdown stringency and longer school closures were associated with larger declines in civic knowledge (Avg. Stringency: −0.035 SD; Days Closed: −0.041 SD). This indicates that stronger and longer school-closure policies may have contributed to measurable deterioration in students’ civic knowledge, though the design is observational and does not establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Trust in civic institutions (INTRUST)
main_findings.target_variable: Trust in civic institutions change (INTRUST scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Separate regressions (standardized coefficients, jackknife SEs). Avg. Stringency: −0.057*** (SE 0.011); Days Closed: −0.076*** (SE 0.012). # Students: 104,088 (INTRUST).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Trust in civic institutions the study leveraged student background controls and country-level pandemic severity measures to estimate associations between COVID-19 lockdown measures and changes in trust, finding that both higher lockdown stringency and longer school closures were associated with larger declines in trust (Avg. Stringency: −0.057 SD; Days Closed: −0.076 SD). This indicates that prolonged or stringent containment policies may erode adolescents’ trust in civic institutions, suggesting that post-lockdown civic trust support and institutional communication could be important for recovery.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected participation in legal protest (LEGACT)
main_findings.target_variable: Expected legal protest participation change (LEGACT scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Separate regressions (standardized coefficients, jackknife SEs). Avg. Stringency: 0.087*** (SE 0.010); Days Closed: 0.031*** (SE 0.008). # Students: 102,824 (LEGACT).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected participation in legal protest the study leveraged student background and country-level pandemic severity controls to estimate how lockdown stringency and school-closure duration relate to changes in expected legal protest participation, finding that higher lockdown stringency and longer closures were associated with increases in expected legal protest participation (Avg. Stringency: 0.087 SD; Days Closed: 0.031 SD). This indicates that more stringent containment may have motivated some students to expect greater civic voice expression through legal protest, implying that civic education and dialogue channels may need strengthening during crises.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected participation in illegal protest (ILLACT)
main_findings.target_variable: Expected illegal protest participation change (ILLACT scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Separate regressions (standardized coefficients, jackknife SEs). Avg. Stringency: 0.041*** (SE 0.010); Days Closed: 0.034*** (SE 0.009). # Students: 102,172 (ILLACT).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected participation in illegal protest the study leveraged student background controls and country-level pandemic severity measures to estimate associations between COVID-19 lockdown measures and changes in expected illegal protest participation, finding that both higher lockdown stringency and longer school closures were associated with increases in expected illegal protest participation (Avg. Stringency: 0.041 SD; Days Closed: 0.034 SD). This indicates that stringent and prolonged containment may be linked to heightened expectations of protest behavior among adolescents, suggesting that crisis governance and youth civic engagement programs should address perceived fairness and institutional trust.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Separate regressions (standardized coefficients, jackknife SEs). Avg. Stringency: 0.006 (SE 0.009, not significant); Days Closed: −0.024** (SE 0.009). # Students: 102,268 (ELECPART).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected electoral participation the study leveraged student background and country-level pandemic severity controls to estimate how lockdown stringency and school-closure duration relate to changes in expected electoral participation, finding no significant association with average lockdown stringency but a negative association with school-closure duration (Days Closed: −0.024 SD). This indicates that longer closures may have reduced students’ expectations of electoral participation, implying that electoral civic education and trust-building may be particularly important after extended school disruptions.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected active political participation (POLPART)
main_findings.target_variable: Expected active political participation change (POLPART scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Separate regressions (standardized coefficients, jackknife SEs). Avg. Stringency: 0.048*** (SE 0.010); Days Closed: 0.026** (SE 0.010). # Students: 102,211 (POLPART).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 & 2022 Grade 8 Expected active political participation the study leveraged student background controls and country-level pandemic severity measures to estimate associations between COVID-19 lockdown measures and changes in expected active political participation, finding that both higher lockdown stringency and longer school closures were associated with increases in expected active political participation (Avg. Stringency: 0.048 SD; Days Closed: 0.026 SD). This indicates that stringent containment may have increased students’ expectations of engaging in conventional political activities, suggesting that post-crisis civic participation pathways should be supported to channel heightened political interest constructively.

data.outcome_summary: The study combines ICCS 2016 and ICCS 2022 Grade 8 civic outcomes with OxCGRT national COVID-19 containment indicators for 14 countries plus a benchmarking subnational entity (Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia). Civic knowledge is PV-based and analyzed using Rubin’s rules, while trust and expected participation outcomes are ICCS linked scales. The authors estimate separate regression models for each civic outcome, using senate sampling weights and jackknife repeated replication for standard errors, and they control for student demographics (gender, age, immigrant status, and socioeconomic background) plus country-level participation/exclusion rates and pandemic severity (case rates and vaccination rates). Across outcomes, lockdown stringency and longer school closures are associated with larger declines in civic knowledge and trust, and with increases (or smaller declines) in expected protest and political participation; electoral participation shows inconsistent results. The paper is observational and does not establish causality, and it uses aggregated country-level lockdown measures that may not capture within-country variation.
